scope_note: Evidence here supports analytical interpretation only. It is not canonical event provenance and does not alter data/sources/registry.json.

evidence.title: Australian economy grew 0.4% in the June quarter
supports: June-quarter 2026 real GDP rose 0.4% quarter-on-quarter.
Real GDP was 2.1% higher than the June quarter of 2025.
The ABS characterised growth as subdued and household behaviour as cautious.

evidence.title: Australia economy slows in Q2 but not by enough to fend off another rate hike
supports: Market forecasts were 0.3% quarter-on-quarter and 1.8% year-on-year GDP growth.
Near-term RBA September-hike pricing rose to 57% from 48% after the release.
Australian ten-year yields were also being pushed by renewed US-Iran fighting, higher oil prices and inflation concerns.
evidence.distribution_note: The linked RTÉ page identifies Reuters as its source. WORLD SIGNALS does not treat this syndication page as authority for canonical event timing.

evidence.provider: Reserve Bank of New Zealand – Te Pūtea Matua
evidence.host_or_distribution: Reserve Bank of New Zealand – Te Pūtea Matua
evidence.title: OCR increased by 25 basis points to 2.75%
supports: The Monetary Policy Committee increased the Official Cash Rate by 25 basis points to 2.75 percent.
The decision was made by consensus.
The Committee said future policy would depend on the balance of risks to medium-term inflation and did not pre-determine the future OCR path.

evidence.title: New Zealand central bank raises rates by 25 bps, flags gradual tightening path
supports: The article reports that 27 of 31 economists polled by Reuters expected a 25 basis point increase to 2.75 percent.
The headline policy action was therefore widely expected before the decision.
evidence.distribution_note: This evidence record is used only to preserve the reported pre-decision Reuters poll benchmark. It does not establish canonical timing or source authority.

evidence.title: NZ dollar skids as RBNZ flags gradual hikes, Aussie supported
supports: Reuters described the 25 basis point increase to 2.75 percent as expected, while characterising the projected future tightening path as more gradual and limited than markets had priced.
The RBNZ projected the OCR at 2.81 percent by December 2026 and 3.15 percent at the end of 2027, while markets had priced a faster pace and a peak around 3.5 percent.
Two-year swap rates fell 3 basis points to 3.7001 percent after the decision.
The New Zealand dollar fell 0.7 percent to US$0.5893.
Longer-term bond yields were simultaneously being lifted by a global sell-off associated with renewed Gulf fighting, higher oil prices and inflation concerns.
evidence.distribution_note: The Business Recorder page identifies Reuters as the source. WORLD SIGNALS uses it as analytical evidence only and does not treat it as canonical RBNZ provenance.

evidence.provider: Ministry of Statistics & Programme Implementation / Press Information Bureau
evidence.host_or_distribution: Press Information Bureau, Government of India
evidence.title: Quarterly Estimates of Gross Domestic Product for the First Quarter (April-June) of 2026-27
supports: Real GDP grew 7.8 percent year-on-year in Q1 FY2026-27.
The release was posted at 4:00 PM India time on 31 August 2026.

evidence.title: India smashes growth forecasts as investment surges in April-June
supports: Reuters reported Q1 FY2026-27 real GDP growth of 7.8 percent year-on-year against economists' projections of 7.1 percent.
The article identifies high oil prices and geopolitical uncertainty as external risks around the growth outlook.

evidence.title: RBI intervention, dollar flows push Indian rupee to two-month peak
supports: The rupee ended at 94.9500 INR per USD, 0.2 percent stronger than the previous close.
Reuters identified RBI dollar-selling intervention and flow-related dollar supply from foreign banks as the principal immediate drivers.
Reuters also reported that the previous day's strong growth data improved sentiment toward the rupee.
Higher global yields, higher oil prices and renewed US-Iran tensions were simultaneous external headwinds.

evidence.title: BI-Rate Held at 5.75%: Strengthening Stability, Supporting Economic Growth
supports: The 18-19 August 2026 Board of Governors Meeting held BI-Rate at 5.75 percent.
The Deposit Facility rate remained 4.75 percent and the Lending Facility rate 6.50 percent.
BI explicitly cited rupiah stability amid heightened global volatility and the Middle East war, inflation within target and sustainable growth.

evidence.title: Indonesia Central Bank Holds Rates Steady at 5.75%, as Expected
supports: All but one of 28 economists polled by Reuters expected BI to hold the benchmark rate at 5.75 percent.
The decision was the first rate-setting meeting under interim governor Destry Damayanti after the prior governor's resignation.
evidence.distribution_note: The Kontan page identifies Reuters as source. It is analytical evidence only and not canonical event provenance.

evidence.title: MPC Press Release 20 August 2026
supports: The overnight deposit rate remained 19.00 percent and overnight lending rate 20.00 percent.
The main-operation and discount rates remained 19.50 percent.
Monthly headline and core inflation were 0.0 percent in July and below expectations.
CBE retained upside-risk warnings around regional hostilities and fiscal-consolidation pass-through.

evidence.title: HC expects the MPC to hold interest rates at its 20 August meeting
supports: HC Securities expected the CBE MPC to keep interest rates unchanged at its 20 August meeting.
Its rationale included accelerated inflation pressure and higher energy costs alongside a comparatively resilient external position.

evidence.title: Índice de precios al consumidor — July 2026 technical report surface
supports: Historical first-party verification in tranche R recorded the 13 August 2026 July CPI technical report and a 2.1 percent month-on-month national CPI increase.
The INDEC URL is a rolling official publication surface; this analytical citation does not replace canonical R provenance.
evidence.distribution_note: Rolling first-party publication surface. The canonical R assertion preserves the historical occurrence verification independently of this analytical record.

evidence.title: Argentina monthly inflation rises in July to 2.1%
supports: July CPI rose 2.1 percent month-on-month versus analyst expectations of 2.0 percent.
June CPI had been 1.9 percent and year-on-year CPI rose to 33.8 percent from 33.5 percent.
Recreation and culture recorded the largest price increases, driven by winter-holiday packages, followed by restaurants and hotels.

evidence.title: Weekly Petroleum Status Report — data for week ending August 28, 2026
supports: The 2 September 2026 WPSR covers the week ending 28 August 2026.
Commercial crude stocks were 428.910 million barrels on 21 August and 424.460 million on 28 August, a 4.450 million-barrel draw.
Distillate stocks were 103.391 million barrels on 21 August and 104.187 million on 28 August, a 0.796 million-barrel build.

evidence.title: US crude stocks fall on strong refining activity and exports, EIA says
supports: A Reuters poll expected a 1.1 million-barrel crude draw and a 1.3 million-barrel distillate draw.
Reuters reported the actual crude draw as about 4.5 million barrels and the distillate change as a roughly 0.8 million-barrel build.
Following the report Brent was up $0.68 to $95.33 and WTI was up $0.35 to $90.57 at 11:01 ET.
The release contained mixed product signals rather than a single-direction inventory surprise.
evidence.distribution_note: The BOE Report page identifies Reuters as source. WORLD SIGNALS uses it as analytical evidence only and does not treat it as canonical EIA provenance.

evidence.title: Oil prices settle up more than $4 a barrel on renewed US-Iran fighting
supports: Oil prices settled more than $4 per barrel higher on 1 September as renewed US-Iran fighting intensified Middle East supply-disruption risk.
Brent settled at $94.65 per barrel, up $4.16 or 4.6 percent, and WTI settled at $90.22, up $4.46 or 5.2 percent.
The pre-existing geopolitical repricing materially contaminates interpretation of the following day's ordinary inventory-release reaction.

evidence.title: Regulation (EU) 2023/1781 — Article 40 evaluation and review
supports: Article 40 requires the Commission to submit the first evaluation and review report to the European Parliament and Council by 20 September 2026 and make it public.
The statutory date is a latest-date obligation, not an assertion that publication must occur exactly on 20 September.

evidence.title: 2026 Commission Work Programme — Annex II annual plan on evaluations and fitness checks
supports: The Evaluation of the Chips Act was listed with an indicative adoption time of Q1 2026.
The timetable was explicitly indicative and is not treated as an exact legal commitment.

evidence.title: SWD(2026) 504 final — Impact Assessment Report accompanying Chips Act 2.0
supports: The impact-assessment package includes the Evaluation of the Chips Act as an annex.
The evaluation examines the first Chips Act across effectiveness, efficiency, relevance, coherence and EU added value and covers implementation through the end of November 2025.
The evaluation was one input into the broader Chips Act 2.0 policy process.

evidence.title: COM(2026) 504 final — Proposal for Chips Act 2.0
supports: The Commission states that the first Article 40 evaluation and review report had been submitted by the statutory deadline.
The proposal summarises findings from the first Chips Act evaluation and places them within the evidence base for Chips Act 2.0.
The proposal also reflects wider impact-assessment, consultation, technological and geopolitical considerations, so the evaluation is not treated as a sole cause of the follow-on proposal.

evidence.provider: Ministry of Finance, Government of Nepal
evidence.host_or_distribution: Ministry of Finance, Government of Nepal
evidence.title: Budget speech archive — FY2083/84 budget statement
supports: The Ministry of Finance budget-speech archive lists the FY2083/84 budget statement with the source-native date 15 Jestha 2083.
The English 2026/27 budget speech is listed separately and later on the archive.
The archive's CMS publication-time field is not evidence of the constitutional budget-presentation clock time and is not used to resolve canonical Gregorian or UTC timing.

evidence.title: Budget to focus on good governance and economic revitalization
supports: Before presentation, Radio Nepal reported that the National Planning Commission had set an NPR 1.89 trillion budget ceiling.
A senior Finance Ministry official was reported as expecting a budget in roughly the NPR 1.89-2.00 trillion range.
The earlier planning envelope is historical expectation context and must not automatically override later pre-event revisions.

evidence.title: Wagle set to unveil large deficit budget above fiscal ceiling
supports: Before presentation, the article reported that the original NPR 1.89 trillion ceiling had been revised on Wednesday to around NPR 2.15 trillion at the Finance Minister's request.
The article described the expected spending plan as roughly NPR 2.1-2.2 trillion.
This later pre-event benchmark supersedes use of the original ceiling as a standalone surprise baseline.

evidence.title: Budget 2026/27: Budget estimates of 2124 billion for the upcoming fiscal year
supports: The announced FY2083/84 budget total was NPR 2,124.34 billion.
Current expenditure was NPR 1,270.58 billion, capital expenditure NPR 431.10 billion and financial management NPR 422.64 billion.
The reported deficit was NPR 657.29 billion, with NPR 247.28 billion planned from foreign loans and NPR 410 billion from internal loans.

evidence.title: NEPSE welcomes budget 2026/27 on negative note, index plunges 26.72 points
supports: On the first trading day after the budget announcement, NEPSE fell 26.72 points and closed at 2,755.37.
The source reports the market opened at 2,782.10, but V preserves the source-reported change and endpoint rather than reconstructing its own event-window baseline.

evidence.title: Capital market reforms draw mixed response as investors flag tax inequities
supports: Market participants welcomed final-tax treatment and some structural capital-market reforms while criticising higher capital-gains tax rates and the absence of portfolio loss offsets.
The article also describes weak corporate performance and hesitant investor demand as pre-existing constraints on market momentum.
The budget therefore contained internally mixed capital-market signals rather than a single-direction equity catalyst.

evidence.provider: Financial Comptroller General Office, Government of Nepal
evidence.title: Daily Receipts & Payments Status — as of 2083-05-18 / 2026-09-03
supports: As of 3 September 2026, the page reported total Treasury expenditure at 5.79 percent of the annual budget.
Recurrent expenditure was 5.69 percent, capital expenditure 1.19 percent and financing 10.78 percent.
The FCGO explicitly warns that the data are unprocessed and subject to change after reconciliation, with direct-payment expenditure only partially included.

evidence.provider: United Nations Office for Disarmament Affairs / Biological Weapons Convention
evidence.title: BWC Meetings — Working Group on the Strengthening of the Convention
supports: The Ninth Review Conference established the Working Group to identify, examine and develop measures, including possible legally-binding measures, and make recommendations to strengthen and institutionalise the Convention.
The Working Group was urged to complete its work as soon as possible, preferably before the end of 2025.
At completion the Working Group is to adopt by consensus a report with conclusions and recommendations for States Parties.

evidence.title: BWC/WG/8/CRP.2 — Draft procedural report of the eighth session
supports: The eighth session continued consideration of measures under agenda item 6.
The Chair issued successive revisions of the draft final report during the session, culminating in Rev.3 on 13 February without prejudice to future discussions.
At the closing meeting on 13 February, the eighth session adopted its procedural report by consensus.

evidence.title: Eighth session (2026) — official document index
supports: The official eighth-session document index lists successive revised draft final reports through BWC/WG/8/CRP.1/Rev.3.
The same index separately lists the procedural report, distinguishing the negotiated draft final-report text from the procedural report adopted for the session.

evidence.title: Working Group on the Strengthening of the Convention — tenth session (2026)
supports: UNODA schedules the tenth Working Group session for 7-11 December 2026 in Geneva.
The scheduled continuation is a future process dependency and not evidence that substantive consensus has already been achieved.

evidence.title: 93rd General Session of the World Assembly of Delegates
supports: The 93rd General Session took place 18-22 May 2026 in Paris.
WOAH reports 35 resolutions adopted and 51 international standards adopted or revised.
WOAH reports 3 new and 9 revised Terrestrial Code chapters, 17 revised Terrestrial Manual chapters, 18 revised Aquatic Code chapters and 4 revised Aquatic Manual chapters.
Six Members had new animal-health statuses recognised and three Members had animal-disease control programmes endorsed.

evidence.title: GS93 — Final resolutions
supports: The final resolution set records the formal resolutions adopted at the 93rd General Session.
Resolution No. 18 concerns the updated Global Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance 2026-2036.
The existence of a formal resolution establishes adoption as an institutional outcome but does not by itself establish national implementation or external impact.

evidence.title: WOAH 8th Strategic Plan adopted for 2027–2031
supports: WOAH Members adopted the 8th Strategic Plan on 20 May 2026 for 2027-2031.
The Plan formally takes effect in 2027.
Its orientations include strengthening global standards, empowering national animal-health systems and elevating animal health as a global priority.
The transition from adoption in 2026 to implementation from 2027 is explicit.

evidence.title: WOAH Members adopt the updated Global Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance
supports: WOAH states that its 183 Members adopted the updated GAP-AMR 2026-2036 on 21 May 2026 through Resolution No. 18.
WOAH characterises the plan as a One Health framework spanning human, animal, plant and environmental health.
WHO Member States subsequently adopted the updated Plan, demonstrating cross-institutional alignment without establishing implementation success.

evidence.title: International Standards
supports: WOAH states that the WTO SPS Agreement encourages WTO Members to base sanitary measures on international standards where they exist.
WOAH identifies itself as the WTO reference organisation for animal-health and zoonosis standards.
The Terrestrial Code supports prevention, detection and control of pathogens and safe international trade in animals and animal products.

evidence.title: The WTO and the World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH)
supports: The WTO identifies WOAH as one of the standard-setting bodies recognised by the SPS Agreement.
WTO-WOAH collaboration concerns the use of international standards in the SPS Agreement context.
The SPS Agreement calls for Members to base sanitary or phytosanitary measures on international standards, guidelines or recommendations on as wide a basis as possible.

evidence.title: Development of Animal Welfare Standards
supports: WOAH states that its animal-welfare standards are internationally recognised science-based standards.
WOAH explicitly distinguishes them from animal-health and veterinary-public-health standards by stating that animal-welfare standards are not recognised in the WTO SPS Agreement.
Therefore the headline count of standards adopted or revised at GS93 cannot be treated as one homogeneous category of SPS-relevant standards.

evidence.title: How WOAH’s new and revised chapters ensure better control of avian influenza
supports: WOAH states that GS93 revised a trade standard and created a new biosecurity chapter relevant to avian influenza.
The changes responded to Member requests and are designed for Members to implement.
Live-bird markets are identified as a particularly vulnerable setting for infectious-disease spread, illustrating a concrete animal-health, biosecurity and trade interface.

evidence.title: 30-Year JGB issue 91 auction issuance notice — 3 September 2026
supports: The Ministry notified auction participants of the 30-year JGB issue 91 auction on 3 September 2026.
The nominal coupon was 4.0 percent and the planned issuance amount was approximately JPY 600 billion.
The notice is official issuance guidance, not a forecast of auction demand or secondary-market response.

evidence.title: Auction Result of 30-Year JGBs on September 3, 2026
supports: Competitive bids totalled JPY 1,728.1 billion and accepted competitive bids totalled JPY 456.2 billion.
The lowest accepted price was 98.65, corresponding to a 4.100 percent yield.
The weighted-average price was 98.93, corresponding to a 4.079 percent yield.
Accepted non-price competitive auction I bids totalled JPY 143.4 billion.

evidence.title: Japan bond yields retreat; 30-year auction uneventful
supports: Reuters described the 30-year auction as largely uneventful as expected.
Bid-to-cover was 3.79 times versus 3.86 at the previous sale and the auction tail was 0.28 versus 0.21 in August.
A strategist said the result looked somewhat weaker than the previous auction on those measures but was not poor against the broader recent average/trend.
The 30-year secondary-market JGB yield was unchanged after the auction and was down 9.5 basis points on the day at 4.070 percent.
The 10-year yield was down 4 basis points at 2.970 percent, while U.S. Treasury, Fed-expectation, yen and BOJ factors were also active.
evidence.distribution_note: The linked Business Recorder page identifies Reuters as the source. It is used for analytical expectation, market observation and context only, not canonical timing.

evidence.title: How Japan's bond rout is turning the tide of global capital
supports: Reuters documented evidence that higher Japanese yields were making domestic bonds more attractive to Japanese investors.
The article described reduced marginal Japanese demand for foreign sovereign debt and possible effects on global term premia.
This is structural context and an observed broader trend; it is not evidence that the 3 September auction caused capital repatriation.

evidence.title: Bank of Canada maintains the policy rate at 2¼%
supports: The target for the overnight rate was maintained at 2.25 percent, Bank Rate at 2.5 percent and the deposit rate at 2.20 percent.
The decision statement identified persistent Middle East conflict, high energy prices and renewed Canada-US tariff measures as material risks.
This official release establishes the policy outcome, not a market expectation or market reaction.

evidence.title: Monetary Policy Decision Press Conference Opening Statement — 2 September 2026
supports: Macklem said recent growth and inflation had evolved broadly as forecast and explained the decision to maintain 2.25 percent.
He said upside risks to inflation had increased as high energy prices persisted, while new tariffs increased uncertainty around growth.
The Bank remained prepared to adjust monetary policy as needed.
The statement supports policy-transmission watch items but does not establish observed market causality.

evidence.title: Bank of Canada to hold rates for another year, wait for more stability on trade: Reuters poll
supports: All 35 economists polled expected the Bank of Canada to hold the overnight rate at 2.25 percent on 2 September, in line with market pricing.
The poll median expected 2.25 percent to persist through at least 2027 Q3, with 2.50 percent in 2027 Q4.
The poll provides a defensible pre-event headline and path benchmark; it is not itself market-movement evidence.

evidence.title: Bank of Canada holds key rate, says multiple hikes might be needed
supports: Reuters reported the 2.25 percent hold was widely expected.

Reuters described the communication as more hawkish, including the removal of earlier language that the current rate was appropriate to balance risks and Macklem's statement that multiple hikes could be needed if inflation remained too high.
Markets moved to price hikes beginning in December and potentially continuing into 2027.
Reuters reported the Canadian dollar rose slightly and Canadian government bond yields edged higher after the remarks.
The report links communication and repricing but does not provide an independently reconstructed exact timestamp market series.

evidence.title: Canadian dollar rebounds from nearly three-week low on BoC rate hike bets
supports: Reuters reported the Canadian dollar 0.4 percent stronger at C$1.3840 per US dollar after earlier touching C$1.3939.
The report said investors raised expectations of future Bank of Canada rate hikes after the Bank emphasised greater upside inflation risks.
RBC strategists said the emphasis on upside inflation risks from energy-price pass-through caught the market off guard.
The reported session move is not an independently reconstructed exact 09:45 pre/post series.

evidence.title: Canadian dollar weakens ahead of BoC rate decision, 10-year yield hits a 2-year high
supports: On 1 September the Canadian dollar weakened 0.4 percent to C$1.3905 per US dollar.
Canada's 10-year government bond yield reached a two-year high amid a broader global bond sell-off.
This establishes material pre-existing FX and rates volatility ahead of the Bank decision and limits monocausal interpretation of 2 September moves.

evidence.title: Australian tropical cyclone season monitoring and planning
supports: The official Australian-region tropical cyclone season runs from 1 November to 30 April.
The Bureau planning climatology states that on average there are about 10 tropical cyclones in the Australian region each season, with 3-4 making landfall, based on seasons since 1980-81.
The Bureau states that tropical cyclone activity varies substantially from year to year; the climatological values are planning context rather than a season-specific point forecast.
The page identifies that cyclones, tropical lows and offshore systems can produce damaging winds, rainfall, flooding, waves, storm surge and coastal impacts.

evidence.host_or_distribution: Bureau of Meteorology Tropical Climate Update archive
evidence.title: Tropical Climate Update — 14 October 2025
supports: The Bureau said tropical cyclone risk increases from November to April, the official season in the Australian region.
The Bureau directed users to its updated tropical cyclone season outlook/planning material and stressed that one cyclone can significantly impact communities.
The update states that tropical lows and cyclones that remain offshore can also cause substantial impacts.
The reviewed archived update does not provide a numerical 2025-26 Australian-region count forecast suitable for a directional forecast-error calculation.

evidence.title: 2025-26 northern wet season
supports: Eleven tropical cyclones formed in or moved into the Australian region during the 2025-26 season, compared with an average of 10 over seasons since 1980-81.
Seven tropical cyclones reached severe intensity, Category 3 or greater, including two Category 5 systems.
Four tropical cyclones made mainland landfall at tropical-cyclone strength and two additional systems crossed at tropical-low strength.

The summary records very warm sea-surface temperatures and above-average northern wet-season rainfall as broader climate context; it does not establish a single-driver causal attribution for the cyclone season.

evidence.host_or_distribution: Bureau of Meteorology news and media
evidence.title: Northern Australia's 2025-26 wet season summary now available
supports: The Bureau described 11 tropical cyclones as close to the average of 10.
The Bureau reported six land crossings across cyclone-strength and tropical-low systems and seven severe tropical cyclones.
Sea-surface temperatures around northern Australia were the fourth warmest on record, while the Coral Sea was the warmest on record for the second consecutive wet season.
These contextual climate observations are not themselves a quantified attribution of the season's cyclone activity or impacts.

evidence.title: Financial Stability Review — March 2026
supports: The RBA assessed risks to the global financial system as having increased amid escalation of conflict in the Middle East and sharp movements in global financial markets.
The RBA assessed Australia's financial system as well placed to handle a challenging and uncertain global environment.
The page identifies heightened operational, cyber and security disruption risk and emphasises continued resilience and prudent lending standards.

evidence.title: Financial Stability Assessment — Financial Stability Review March 2026
supports: The Review was finalised on 18 March 2026 while the Middle East conflict was evolving rapidly.
The RBA states that escalation of the conflict sparked a substantial increase in volatility after a lengthy period of unusually low risk premia.

The RBA identifies leverage and concentration in global markets, sovereign-debt repricing, NBFI amplification, cyber and operational risks and multiple channels through which severe global stress could affect Australia.
The identified transmission channels are conditional financial-stability mechanisms, not outcomes caused by publication of the Review.

evidence.title: Financial Stability Assessment — Financial Stability Review October 2025
supports: The October 2025 Review already assessed global financial-stability risks as elevated and highlighted sovereign debt, low risk premia, NBFI leverage and liquidity mismatches, operational and cyber vulnerabilities, and China-related spillover risks.
It described market volatility as having subsided from the April episode, providing an institutional baseline for comparison with March 2026.
This prior official assessment is context and prior guidance, not evidence of a consensus forecast for the March 2026 FSR's exact contents.

evidence.title: Australia central bank hikes rates to 10-month high as Iran war stokes inflation risk
supports: The RBA raised the cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.10 percent on 17 March in a 5-4 decision.
Reuters reported Australian-dollar, bond-futures and policy-path repricing around that decision and Governor Bullock's explanation.
The report identifies domestic inflation and the Middle East oil shock as major contemporaneous drivers, establishing material Australia-specific market information before the FSR release.

evidence.title: Euro and yen gain, pushing dollar index lower following central bank decisions
supports: Reuters reported broad FX moves on 19 March after multiple major central-bank decisions and continuing Middle East-driven oil volatility.
It reported the Australian dollar higher on the day while foregrounding Australian labour data and the RBA's earlier tightening cycle, not the Financial Stability Review as the driver.
The article establishes a heavily contaminated same-session market environment and does not supply an independently reconstructed 11:30 AEDT FSR event window.

evidence.provider: National Election Commission of the Republic of Korea
evidence.host_or_distribution: National Election Commission Policy & Pledge portal
evidence.title: 9th Nationwide Simultaneous Local Elections — elected-candidate/winner portal
supports: The NEC winner/elected-candidate surface establishes that the 9th Nationwide Simultaneous Local Elections produced elected candidates and were completed as an electoral process.
The official surface represents many local contests rather than a single national partisan outcome.
This Analysis evidence does not alter the canonical source identity or timing already established upstream.

evidence.title: South Korea Lee's ruling party sweeps local elections, but loses Seoul mayor race
supports: Reuters reported that the Democratic Party won 12 of 16 major mayoral/provincial contests and the People Power Party won four.
The PPP retained Seoul under incumbent Oh Se-hoon while the DP won Busan.
The report also identifies local and national political context relevant to interpreting the distributed result.

evidence.title: Ruling party wins landslide in local elections despite losing Seoul to incumbent mayor
supports: Yonhap independently reported the 12-to-4 split across the 16 major mayoral and gubernatorial contests.
Yonhap reported DP victory in Busan and PPP retention of Seoul.
The corroboration supports the aggregate contest-class description without turning the full nationwide election into a single result.

evidence.title: South Korea heads to local elections under shadow of disgraced former president
supports: Reuters reported that analysts expected the conservatives to suffer a severe or landslide defeat in the June local elections.

The PPP entered the election controlling 12 of 16 major local governments, while late-April Gallup Korea support was reported at 46 percent for the DP versus 21 percent for the PPP and 64 percent approval for President Lee.
The report establishes directional pre-election political context but does not provide an exact contest-distribution forecast.

evidence.title: South Korea ruling party set for local election gains, exit poll shows
supports: The joint broadcasters' post-vote exit poll projected the DP ahead in 11 of 16 major mayoral/provincial races and projected a DP Seoul win.
Because the exit poll was produced after voting, it is observation context rather than an ex-ante expectation benchmark.
The difference between exit-poll projection and final result illustrates post-vote uncertainty without creating pre-event forecast error.

evidence.title: NEC says supplemental ballots sent to 140 polling stations; voting interrupted at 26
supports: Yonhap reported the NEC's updated accounting that supplemental ballots were sent to 140 of 14,288 polling stations.
The supplemental papers were actually used at 91 polling stations and voting was temporarily interrupted then resumed at 26.
The NEC established an external fact-finding committee to examine ballot printing, allocation, supply management and response procedures.

evidence.title: How South Korea's ballot shortage spurred turnout of thousands to defend democracy
supports: Reuters documented sustained protests and rerun demands following the ballot shortages.
The report recorded the resignation of NEC chief Rho Tae-ak and President Lee's investigation and reform response.
It also documents fraud allegations and pre-existing mistrust as political claims/context rather than adjudicated findings.

evidence.title: South Korea's Lee calls for overhaul of election management after flawed vote
supports: President Lee called for major reform of election management after the ballot-paper shortage controversy.
He ordered a probe involving prosecutors and police and raised possible legal or constitutional reform if political agreement existed.
The report supports an observed institutional-response chain while not establishing that the administration failure caused the partisan election result.

evidence.title: June Climate Meetings (SB64) official event page
supports: The UN June Climate Meetings (SB64) were held in Bonn from 8 to 18 June 2026.
The official page recorded on 18 June that the June Climate Meetings had officially closed.
The page links the distinct SBI 64 and SBSTA 64 session surfaces rather than establishing one merged legal body.

evidence.title: Written statement of UNFCCC Executive Secretary on closing of UN June Climate Meetings (SB64)
supports: The Executive Secretary stated that significant divides and significant intersessional work remained at closure.
The statement identified progress in key areas, including steps on just transition.
The statement is institutional interpretation/context rather than a Party-adopted consensus decision text.

evidence.title: UN Climate Change Quarterly Update: Q2 2026
supports: UNFCCC characterises SB64 as delivering mixed results and progress, with good headway on several key issues and inadequate progress on others.
The update identifies progress on just transition, Action for Climate Empowerment and implementation of global stocktake outcomes, alongside work on finance, technology and capacity-building.
This is a post-event synthesis and not an ex-ante surprise benchmark.

evidence.title: SBI 64 session page and post-session reports
supports: SBI 64 is a distinct subsidiary-body session held in Bonn from 8 to 18 June 2026 with its own agenda and mandated workstreams.
UNFCCC published FCCC/SBI/2026/15 and addenda on 28 August 2026.
FCCC/SBI/2026/15/Add.1 contains draft decisions forwarded for consideration and adoption by the relevant higher UNFCCC bodies.
Forwarding a draft is a future-decision input and does not itself establish later adoption.

evidence.provider: UNFCCC Subsidiary Body for Scientific and Technological Advice
evidence.title: SBSTA 64 session page and post-session reports
supports: SBSTA 64 is a distinct subsidiary-body session held in Bonn from 8 to 18 June 2026 with its own agenda and workstreams.
UNFCCC published FCCC/SBSTA/2026/5 and FCCC/SBSTA/2026/5/Add.1 on 28 August 2026.
The addendum contains draft decisions forwarded for consideration and adoption by the relevant higher UNFCCC bodies.
The separate report series preserves SBSTA's legal/institutional identity rather than merging it into SBI.

evidence.title: WHA79 governing-body archive, journals, resolutions and decisions
supports: WHA79 was held from 18 to 23 May 2026 and has a formal archive of journals, resolutions, decisions and recorded-vote outcomes.
The archive shows that WHA79 contained many legally and substantively distinct decisions rather than one unitary outcome.
The archive is the controlling first-party decision record for the Assembly-level analysis.

evidence.title: Seventy-ninth World Health Assembly daily update: 23 May 2026
supports: WHO states that Member States adopted more than 20 decisions and 13 resolutions during WHA79.
WHO records the closing of the Assembly on 23 May 2026.
The update summarises technical, political and administrative outputs without making decision count a scalar impact metric.

evidence.title: WHO Member States agree to extend negotiations on Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing annex
supports: Before WHA79, WHO stated that PABS negotiations had progressed but additional time was needed.
WHO stated that WHA79 would be asked to consider continuing the IGWG work and submitting the outcome to WHA80 or an earlier special session.
This is official prior guidance for the PABS workstream, not an aggregate forecast for all WHA79 decisions.

evidence.title: WHA79(7): Outcome of the IGWG in relation to the Article 12 PABS Annex
supports: WHA79 decided that the IGWG shall continue its work and prioritise drafting and negotiating the PABS Annex.
The decision requires the outcome to be submitted to WHA80 or, if necessary, an earlier special session in 2026.
Continuation of negotiation is distinct from adoption of the Annex and from later signature, ratification or implementation of the Pandemic Agreement.

evidence.title: WHA79(20): Reform of the global health architecture and the UN80 Initiative
supports: WHA79 established the proposed joint process to support reforms of the global health architecture.
The decision specifies later task-force, consultation, interim-report and final-report stages extending into WHA80 in 2027.
Establishment of the reform process is not evidence that the intended reform outcomes were already achieved at WHA79.

evidence.title: World Health Assembly adopts updated Global Action Plan on antimicrobial resistance 2026-2036
supports: WHO states that Member States at WHA79 adopted the updated Global Action Plan on antimicrobial resistance 2026-2036 on 23 May 2026.
The plan provides a One Health framework intended to guide coordinated action over the following decade.
Formal plan adoption does not itself establish implementation or realised health outcomes.

evidence.title: WHO Member States continue negotiations on the Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing Annex
supports: The seventh IGWG meeting took place on 6-17 July 2026 after WHA79 continued the negotiating mandate.
WHO reported that negotiations advanced but further discussions remained necessary to finalise the PABS Annex.
WHO scheduled an eighth IGWG meeting for 14-18 September 2026, showing continuing process propagation without substantive completion by the AP reference date.

evidence.title: Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine: Council extends economic sanctions for another year
supports: The Council states that it renewed the economic restrictive measures on 25 June 2026 for a further twelve months, until 31 July 2027.
The Council states that the renewal followed agreement by EU leaders at the June European Council.
The press release describes the continuing sanctions framework and the EU's readiness to take additional measures.

evidence.title: Council Decision (CFSP) 2026/1437 of 25 June 2026 amending Decision 2014/512/CFSP concerning restrictive measures in view of Russia's actions destabilising the situation in Ukraine
supports: The binding Council decision was done at Brussels on 25 June 2026.
Article 1 amends Article 9(1) so that the measures apply until 31 July 2027.
Article 2 provides that the decision enters into force on the day following publication in the Official Journal.

evidence.title: EU leaders agree to renew Russia sanctions for 12 months
supports: Before the 25 June binding act, Reuters reported that EU leaders had agreed to renew the sanctions for another twelve months.
Reuters described the annual renewal as the first full-year rollover after previous six-month renewals.
The report supplies a contemporaneous political-agreement benchmark, not a binding legal act or market-consensus probability.

evidence.title: European Council conclusions on Ukraine and security and defence, 18 June 2026
supports: The European Council documented continuing pressure on Russia, including energy revenues, the shadow fleet, banking constraints and enforcement.
The conclusions called for swift adoption of a further sanctions package.
This is wider policy context and is not promoted into the binding 25 June renewal act.

evidence.title: Oil prices extend decline on expectations of smoother crude flows via Hormuz
supports: Reuters reported substantial oil-price declines immediately before the Council renewal.
The reported drivers centred on changing expectations about Strait of Hormuz crude flows and Iran-related supply conditions.
This supplies a strong contemporaneous alternative driver and does not establish an EU-renewal market response.

evidence.title: 21st package of sanctions: EU hits Russian energy, financial services and crypto hard
supports: The Council adopted a later 21st sanctions package with additional designations and measures affecting energy, financial services, crypto and the shadow fleet.
The later package demonstrates that the sanctions regime remained capable of amendment and calibration inside the annual legal horizon.
The later package is a distinct act and is not treated as an effect caused by the 25 June renewal.

evidence.host_or_distribution: India Meteorological Department / Ministry of Earth Sciences
evidence.title: Updated Seasonal outlook for hot weather season (April to June) 2026 and Monthly Outlook for April 2026 for the Rainfall and Temperature
supports: IMD published the updated April-June 2026 hot-weather outlook on 31 March 2026.
The release forecast above-normal heatwave days over parts of eastern, central and northwestern India and the southeast peninsula during April-June.
The release identifies public-health, water, power-demand, essential-service, infrastructure/resource-management and agricultural risk channels and preparedness measures.

evidence.host_or_distribution: India Meteorological Department / Ministry of Earth Sciences
evidence.title: Seasonal outlook for the hot weather season March to May 2026 and Monthly Outlook for March 2026
supports: Before the 31 March update, IMD had already forecast above-normal heatwave days over broad parts of east/east-central India, the southeast peninsula and some northwest/west-central areas for March-May 2026.
The prior product uses a March-May reference window and therefore is official prior guidance rather than a matched April-June forecast-error benchmark.
The prior release also identifies public-health, water, power-demand and essential-service risk channels.

evidence.host_or_distribution: India Meteorological Department / Ministry of Earth Sciences
evidence.title: Monthly Outlook for the Temperature and Rainfall during May 2026
supports: IMD issued a May-specific temperature, rainfall and heatwave outlook after the March seasonal product.
The May outlook expected above-normal heatwave days over parts of Himalayan foothills, east-coast states, Gujarat and Maharashtra.
The monthly product is subsequent forecast information, not a verifying observation for the March seasonal forecast.

evidence.title: IMD late-May 2026 heatwave operational press-release sequence
supports: The IMD archive records repeated late-May heatwave/severe-heatwave continuation releases for central, northwestern and eastern India.
A 29 May release states that the prevailing heatwave had abated from most parts of northwest India and was likely to abate from most of central India.
The sequence shows operational weather conditions changing within the seasonal reference period; it is not a national seasonal forecast-skill score.

evidence.host_or_distribution: India Meteorological Department / Ministry of Earth Sciences
evidence.title: Monthly rainfall and temperature outlook for June 2026 — heatwave outlook section
supports: The June outlook expected above-normal heatwave days over many parts of several northern, eastern, central and peninsular states, with below-normal heatwave days likely in Rajasthan and Jharkhand.
The June product demonstrates continuing monthly forecast evolution inside the broader April-June seasonal reference period.
It is not treated as a verifying observation for the March seasonal product.

evidence.host_or_distribution: India Meteorological Department / Ministry of Earth Sciences
evidence.title: IMD operational press release — 21 June 2026
supports: The late-June operational release describes heatwave conditions in isolated pockets across several states during the forecast interval and severe heatwave conditions in isolated pockets of Vidarbha for part of the period.
The release supplies later operational weather context within the April-June reference period.
A short-horizon operational release is not a complete verifying dataset or skill metric for the March seasonal forecast.

evidence.title: Summary of the Latest Month on Family Income and Expenditure Survey — July 2026
supports: July 2026 two-or-more-person household monthly consumption expenditure was JPY 301,245.
Nominal consumption expenditure was down 1.5% year on year and real consumption expenditure was down 3.6% year on year.
Workers' household monthly income was JPY 689,476, down 3.8% year on year in real terms.
The page identifies the July 2026 survey as released on 4 September 2026 without supplying a clock time.
evidence.distribution_note: Civil-date publication evidence only; it does not resolve the Canonical release to a clock time or UTC timestamp.

evidence.title: Family Income and Expenditure Survey monthly results — July 2026
supports: July 2026 real consumption expenditure was down 3.6% year on year and up 0.5% month on month on a seasonally adjusted basis.
The Statistics Bureau explicitly identifies April, May and June 2026 real-change figures as retrospectively revised because of the CPI 2025-base revision.
The revised monthly sequence shown is April -0.5% y/y and +1.5% m/m SA; May -0.4% and +3.5%; June -3.3% and -6.3%; July -3.6% and +0.5%.
evidence.distribution_note: Used to preserve data-vintage/revision context. It does not create a synthetic prior Live observation or alter Canonical provenance.

evidence.title: Family Income and Expenditure Survey notice — CPI 2025-base retrospective revision
supports: On 7 July 2026 the Statistics Bureau announced that, with the July 2026 FIES results scheduled for release on 4 September, real-change figures for prior 2026 months would be retrospectively revised following the CPI 2025-base revision.
The rebasing boundary was therefore known before the July-data release and must not be treated as an ex-post analytical surprise.
evidence.distribution_note: Official pre-release notice used only to establish the known data-vintage boundary; it does not alter Canonical timing or create a Live observation.

evidence.title: Japan July household spending falls at fastest pace in 2-1/2 years
supports: Reuters reported a market forecast for real household spending of -1.6% year on year versus the actual -3.6%.
Reuters reported a seasonally adjusted month-on-month expectation of +2.6% versus the actual +0.5%.
Reuters described the year-on-year fall as the eighth consecutive monthly decline and the steepest since January 2024.
Reuters reported consumer selectivity amid higher living costs and noted household-spending data as relevant context ahead of the Bank of Japan meeting.
evidence.distribution_note: Analytical benchmark/context only. The Reuters URL date reflects its web publication path and is not used to retime the Canonical 4 September Asia/Tokyo release.

evidence.provider: United Nations Office at Geneva / Indico.UN
evidence.title: Ninth Session of the Working Group on the Strengthening of the Biological Weapons Convention
supports: The ninth session of the Working Group on the Strengthening of the Biological Weapons Convention took place in Geneva from 17 to 21 August 2026.

The ninth session is observed institutional follow-through after the February 2026 eighth session; occurrence of the meeting does not itself establish substantive consensus or adoption of a final package.
